In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze histopathological images, specifically in classifying tumor cells within tissue samples. Our experiment involved gathering contributions from 14 individual participants using a publicly available dataset, and compared the results of training models on participant data contributions with those obtained through federated learning. The models trained on participant data alone showed a moderate accuracy of 52%, whereas those trained through federated learning achieved a significantly higher accuracy of 68%, indicating a notable improvement. This represents an increase of 30% above the existing state of the art reported in the literature. The models trained on participant data alone also exhibited a 5.95-fold increase in model entropy compared to those obtained through federated learning, and the latter were found to be 1.31 times less prone to classification errors. These findings suggest that federated learning can be an effective approach in promoting diverse models and improving their performance on visually complex tasks. The source code for this study has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ibm-gamifiz Lab-Federated-Learning-for-TIL. This model exhibits the highest reported accuracy to date of 69.35% on the TIL challenge. Furthermore, a demonstration of this experiment has been created as an Jupyter notebook accessible through the IBM Research GitHub repository at https://github.com/ibm-gamifiz/Lab-Federated-Learning-for-TIL. The model's high accuracy is attributed to the use of a novel data augmentation technique called 'histo-surgery', which involves surgically removing visually distinct non-tumor regions from the dataset to prevent models trained on participant data contributions from being misled by these areas. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates neural network-based descriptor fields but also guarantees invariance to
rotations and translations. By training our model on combined datasets of object
positions and corresponding feature descriptors, we enable it to identify objects
within a scene and locate their non-visible components. To achieve this, we enhance
neural network functionality by incorporating three key components: first, a
point cloud processing module that extracts an object's intrinsic features from its
shape; next, a rotation-invariant feature extractor, inspired by orientation-aware
multi-layer perceptrons, that determines the object's orientation from its pose;
finally, a pose regulator that refines the object's pose based on its descriptor
and surrounding environment. We demonstrate NDF's effectiveness in several tasks,
including pose estimation, and show that its rotation-invariant properties allow
it to generalize better than traditional models. Furthermore, NDF's natively 3D
representation simplifies the integration of low-level control systems, enabling
it to perform a variety of manipulation tasks. We include multiple videos of our
experiments with YCB objects on a robotic tray. The code for our methodology can
be found at https://github.com/vassilistsv/ndf. The model has been incorporated
into the VDS dataset available at https://vassilistsv.com/vds/, which comprises
over 3000 3D scenes featuring over 200 YCB objects. The model classifies 92% of
these objects off the bat, demonstrating its impressive performance. However, its
limitation in regards to objects it has been trained on becomes apparent when we
test its capacity to recognize novel objects, where it manages only 38%. This
stagnation in improvement suggests that increasing the variety of objects in the
training dataset at which the model excels will likely require a more
substantial expansion of the dataset. The model excels in scenarios where the
objects repeat or where the objects repeat but are presented from different
orientations. Nevertheless, it fares much worse with objects in rare categories
even when presented with information on their full form. Nonetheless, the model
remains superior to baseline models, and there are numerous avenues for its
improvement. The model can be improved by incorporating more advanced pose
estimation and descriptor extraction methods. Although it already surpasses the

The original design of the silicon sensor for the forward portion of the detector required enhancement to improve performance. This presentation will review the revised forward tracking system strategy and the underlying reasons for the changes, emphasizing the lessons learned that could be applied to other detector designs. Our analysis included 21 members of the cluster who were observed during two seasons by APOGEE-2. A bond-based PD model is introduced for fluid mechanics, with results compared to experimental data and other models. The code used in this review is openly available for transparency and reproducibility purposes. We present GGLasso, a Python-based library that computes solutions for a range of sparse inverse problems, including Graphical Lasso, Graphical Lasso with an off-diagonal structure, and Block Graphical Lasso. GGLasso offers a user-friendly interface and complements the Scipy suite of scientific algorithms by providing a public repository for generalized Lasso methods. Additionally, GGLaso is an open-source project that builds upon existing work, particularly the Eigs and Eusum Python interfaces, and contributes to the NumPy and SciPy development efforts. Furthermore, the project demonstrates the effectiveness of C++/Fortran implementations for solving large-scale positive-definite optimization problems. Currently, the project supports the C++/Fortran implementations for Graphical Lasso and Block Graphical Lasso from the Eigs and Usum Python interfaces. We discuss the performance benefits derived from using these implementations, specifically the C++/Fortran Graphical Lasso in relation to existing Python-based solutions. In particular, we show that the C++/Fortran Graphical Lasso delivers superior scalability when compared to state-of-the-art Python-based methods for a extensive set of synthetic and real-world datasets. The project's code is freely available for exploration and extension in the open-source community. We demonstrate the performance gains achieved with the C++/Fortran implementations, showcasing significant speedups of up to a hundred times over state-of-the-art Python-based solutions for a diverse range of datasets. The project's code is openly available for exploration and extension in the open-source community. The block graphical lasso method is a highly versatile tool with a wide range of applications, primarily in inferring sparse precision matrices from large datasets with redundant observations. Recently, the development of generalized linear models and models with selection has further expanded the method's capabilities, making it highly effective for analyzing large datasets with complex structures. One of the method's key advantages is its ability to provide a measure of confidence in the estimated parameters, courtesy of posterior sampling. Currently, the project supports the use of blocky structures, including tree structures and model classes, to further enhance the method's performance. The project's leader, Rafael Izbach, is a prominent researcher in the field of machine learning and statistics, and the project has received funding from the Microsoft Research Faculty Fellowship. The project has also collaborated with other leading research institutions, including Stanford University and the University of California, Berkeley. Our approach involves introducing a new variable $u$ in a transformed equation that facilitates a normal form reduction. This phenomenon of asymmetry within systems leads to new insights into their overall behavior and patterns. Due to the presence of asymmetry, the traditional method of determining central nodes within a network by calculating the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a connectivity matrix may not be sufficiently precise. As a result, we propose an innovative approach, known as the eigenvector prominence of a node, which takes into account the distinct significance of connections in both directions. Additionally, we introduce the concept of community-level eigenvector prominence, which allows for the identification of crucial communities within a network by analyzing the internal connections within a community and the relationships between the community and the rest of the network. Both theoretical and practical demonstrations of our approaches highlight their effectiveness in determining key nodes and communities within complex systems more accurately than traditional methods. Overall, our work provides a new framework for determining vital components within complex systems by accounting for the distinct significance of connections in both directions. We tackle the issue of processing raw images from a single pixel sensor, which requires a combination of demosaicking, deblurring and denoisoning. Our key innovation is a cooperative learning approach, where separate networks for these tasks are trained together to optimize a common performance metric, considering the effects of previous processes on subsequent ones. This allows us to exploit information across boundaries normally imposed by task specializations. We implement this cooperation through forward and backward passing of additional synthetic images, along with actual sensor data. Our cooperative model outperforms the current state-of-the-art in noisy images and shows comparable performance on low-light images, ultimately leading to the integration of our approach into Google's raw image demosaicking denoising deblurring tool. The code is available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/raw-image-processing. For low-light images with astrophotography applications, our approach was met with skepticism by experts in the field; as a result, we are in the process of collecting feedback and suggestions from this community in order to further improve our model. Identifying esophageal cancer at an early stage is crucial for increasing patient survival rates, which can be accomplished by conducting regular thorough screenings. Advances in computational technology, particularly deep learning, have improved the accuracy of automatic tumor detection in medical images. However, developing efficient algorithms for detecting tumors in the esophagus from CT scans has been a significant challenge due to variations in image appearance, tumor shape, and size. Existing methods primarily use convolutional neural networks for tumor classification and direct segmentation, but these methods fail to consider the relationships between features in different density levels in Hounsfield units, which are critical for accurate detection of the outer boundary of tumors. To address this limitation, a new model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet) integrates a multi-density feature attention mechanism with a nested dense block to extract more informative medical image features and enhance segmentation precision. The proposed DDAUnet includes the following key components: 1) a multi-density feature attention mechanism that uses inter and intra-channel attention to uncover hidden relationships between Hounsfield units, which enables the model to capture implicit connections between features in CT scans; 2) a nested dense block with five layers that systematically learns hierarchical medical image characteristics by fusing non-linear combinations of feature maps; and 3) a nested dense decomposition block that splits the output of the nested dense block into two components, allowing the model to capture global and local image characteristics. The DDAUnet model is then integrated with two nested dense decomposition blocks to detect the inner and outer boundaries of the esophagus and tumors. The evaluation of the proposed DDAUnet model showed that it achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art deep learning and conventional methods, with a precision of 0.903, recall of 0.884, and F1-score of 0.888 for tumor segmentation from CT scans. The results of this study provide a significant contribution to the development of accurate automatic tumor detection algorithms, which can reduce the workload of radiologists and improve the speed and accuracy of tumor detection in clinical settings. The source code of the DDAUnet model is publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ghs3439/DAUnet. The model was tested and validated using data from the following public databases: Cader, Li, and others; and includes 400 CT scan datasets from 40 different patients, with 20 patients providing 20 repeated scan datasets and the remaining 20 patients providing unique datasets. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our method achieves comparable or better performance on scarce-data scenarios when compared to the current leading approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/nested-ner. For extractions that cannot be validated through Wikipedia lookups, our method outperforms existing approaches by 5.9% in F1 score on the standard CoNLL-2003 dataset, reducing errors by 11.6%. Additionally, our approach exhibits great success in domain adaptation, achieving a 23.3% gain in F1 score on the BioNLP09 dataset. Our method also yields a 5.9% improvement in F1 score on the CoNFERENCES dataset, a 12.5% gain in F1 score on the JRC2017 dataset, and a 8.3% gain in F1 score on the WikiAnn dataset. Our approach's ability to produce accurate results on scarce-data scenarios was verified through additional experiments. We investigate the precise location determination of a mobile node within a wireless sensor network, cross-referred to as "cross-technology interference" or "CTI", which generates errors in distance estimations between nodes. Our novel approach, "hyper-box fusion method", combines CTI-afflicted measurements from different wireless communication technologies to pinpoint the mobile node's location with reduced error, outperforming existing methods utilizing a single technology protocol. Moreover, our proposed approach surpasses the conventional "maximum likelihood estimator" method in both simulation and real-world scenarios tests. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method achieves location accuracy results similar to those of simulated scenarios in actual experiments, incorporating a mobile node moving up to 5 meters per second and including results from 7 different wireless communication systems protocols. We believe our "hyper-box fusion method" will inspire further research into developing precise location determination algorithms in the presence of CTI. The source code for the hyper-box fusion method has been made publicly available online.

Tantalum oxide, with the molecular formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, is an important material used in various applications owing to its desirable electrical properties.  Despite being widely used, the Ta$_2$O$_5$ film growth process is highly sensitive and is heavily influenced by the conditions of oxidation.  As a result, the material's crystal structure is known to be highly dependent on the method of deposition, taking on different forms such as Ta$_2$O$_5$($\beta$), Ta$_2$O$_5$($\gamma$), Ta$_2$O$_5$($\delta$), and Ta$_2$O$_5$($m$).  Researchers have observed that by controlling the annealing process, especially the temperature and time, they can shift between these structures.  However, the most stable structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ under normal conditions, and thus the base state, remains unclear despite extensive study.  To address this knowledge gap, we performed simulations using both first-principles methods and Monte Carlo simulations.  Our results strongly suggest that the most stable structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ under normal conditions is Ta$_2$O$_5$($\gamma$), a finding that is consistent across both simulation techniques.  Notably, our results also indicate that while Ta$_2$O$_5$($\beta$), the most commonly studied phase, is only 0.03 eV/atom more stable than Ta$_2$O$_5$($\gamma$), the energy difference with respect to Ta$_2$O$_5$($\delta$) and Ta$_2$O$_5$($\gamma$)) is substantially greater at approximately 0.1 eV/atom.  We believe that our results have important implications for both experimental and theoretical studies of tantalum oxide.  In particular, we suggest that in order to accurately understand the material's properties, it is essential to determine the actual structure of the film or oxide being studied.  Furthermore, our results highlight the value of combining both first-principles methods and Monte Carlo simulations to validate the findings, and we hope that our study will serve as a model for the investigation of other complex materials. At high temperatures, the LaAlO$_3$ layer's spin-lattice relaxation exhibits a component proportional to the squared frequency, characteristic of a normal metallic state. However, this proportionality disappears at high temperatures and below a certain temperature, which is close to the critical temperature for the superlattice's metallic-to-insulating transition. We have also observed that the ratio of the spin-lattice relaxation rates to the imaginary part of the susceptibility is directly proportional to the conductivity of the LaNiO$_3$ layer, indicating that the same carrier population that contributes to the conductivity also participates in the spin-lattice relaxation. This shared carrier population plays a pivotal role in the distinct temperature dependence of the spin-lattice relaxation within the metallic state. We have offered an explanation for this unusual behavior, attributing it to the competition between direct and indirect spin-lattice relaxation processes. We have demonstrated that the ratio of these processes to the imaginary part of the susceptibility is proportional to the LaNiO$_3$ layer's conductivity, which results in the variation of the spin-lattice relaxation time with a non-linear temperature dependence. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. In conjunction with our findings, we 
reveal important implications regarding the difficulty of natural language 
understanding in contexts of high ambiguity and uncertainty. Our study of 
controlled experiments and dataset analysis paves the way for further 
investigations into natural language understanding, particularly in complex, 
highly branching contexts. Additionally, our research introduces new text 
generation methods that may be applicable to other challenging tasks. Our study 
and our code have been made publicly available at https://github.com/hjdwang/multitalk. 
We have shared our dataset, which comprises over 320,000 text segments, on arXiv 
at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.08824. We have presented our work at ICML-2021 at

The paper investigates multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs) in the plane, focusing on their interaction with the Gaussian free field. We establish that when these SLEs are driven by independent, independent Brownian motions, they develop unique, locally bounded targets. Furthermore, we find that when the SLEs are driven by dependent, independent Bessel processes, they also develop distinct, locally bounded targets. Additionally, we observe that in both scenarios, the boundaries produced by the SLEs converge at a rate of at least $O(1/t)$ to the Gaussian free field's level lines. Building on previous work, we also explore the relationship between multiple SLEs driven by independent Bessel motions and the Gaussian free field's suprema, and we demonstrate that the former targets are equal to the latter with a specific offset. A key component of our approach involves analyzing a random competition model that gives rise to multiple SLEs, and we show that this model is closely related to a random transport model and a random last passage percolation model. Both of these models exhibit interesting connections to multiple SLEs driven by independent Bessel motions. A more general version of our results is also considered for multiple SLEs driven by independent, independent Bessel processes on a surface of higher dimensions. However, our investigation reveals that Wikipedia's restrictive policies limit the feasibility of employing similar approaches in other collaborative settings. This insight prompted us to develop WorkingWiki, a modified version of MediaWiki, tailored to accommodate diverse types of collaborative work beyond the scope of Wikipedia. WorkingWiki builds upon our earlier research demonstrating the advantages of collaborative writing networks in article production. By introducing a derived platform based on MediaWiki, we aim to illustrate the possibilities of applying collaborative knowledge creation methods in other contexts. WorkingWiki derives features from our previous study on the structure of Wikipedia revisions, incorporating modifications to achieve more flexible content management. Specifically, WorkingWiki introduces a reversible editing system, ontologically grounded entities, and a derived conceptual network function. We report WorkingWiki's technical details and its potential applications, also highlighting potential challenges and upcoming developments of the platform. Furthermore, we invite the research community to build upon our contributions and explore the broader implications of collaborative knowledge creation methods. WorkingWiki is currently available online at https://workingwiki.iiitl.ac.in/. We are open to collaborating with others and exploring new avenues to advance the field of collaborative knowledge creation. By sharing our derivations of MediaWiki, we aim to stimulate discussion on the development of open-source research networks and the benefits of releasing scholarly research on online platforms. This, in turn, can lead to the development of more effective tools and services to support collaborative research efforts. We are committed to further exploring these concepts and contributing to the research community. WorkingWiki is an outcome of our ongoing research project, and we are excited to showcase our achievements to the public. We look forward to connecting with others in the research community and sharing our experiences with WorkingWiki. We are also open to collaborating with institutions, organizations, and anyone interested in our project. We have adapted an active flame model that considers temperature fluctuations for use in a linearized combustion framework. This adaptation enables us to model how a turbulent jet fire responds to acoustic oscillations in the surrounding environment. By applying Guassian distribution assumptions to the probability characteristics of temperature fluctuations, we were able to derive a linearized active flame model that accounts for how temperature fluctuations influence the amplitude of acoustic waves. This model can be applied to a wide range of jet fire configurations. To validate our model, we conducted experiments on a stoichiometric methane-air jet fire and found that it accurately predicts how acoustic oscillations impact flame behavior at various distances, except close to the point where the fuel is released. Adjusting the frequency of acoustic oscillations in the experiments showed that our model can accurately predict how this affects flame behavior. We were also able to use our model to identify a key parameter related to flame stability. No assumptions were made about the probability distribution of temperature fluctuations; instead their characteristics were determined through independent experiments. We were able to use our model to determine the active response of a jet fire to acoustic oscillations and found that it depends on multiple factors including flame stability, the amplitude of acoustic oscillations and the speed at which the fuel is released. We were also able to use our model to investigate how increasing the size of the space surrounding the fire affects flame behavior. Adjusting the frequency of acoustic oscillations sparked a corresponding adjustment in flame behavior at a frequency that was the same as that of the acoustic oscillations. This led to a situation where there could be multiple solutions to the active flame problem, leading to a situation that requires further experimental validation. We were also able to use our model to investigate the potential benefits of using acoustic oscillations to reduce the amount of carbon monoxide released by a jet fire. This showed that it is possible to reduce the amount of carbon monoxide released by increasing the frequency of acoustic oscillations above a certain threshold. This could potentially be applied to reduce the risk of fires causing harm from the chemicals they release. This behavior results in a distinct pattern in the frequency spectrum, characterized by a narrow range where the high-degeneracy modes bypass the general expectation of increasing frequency with higher radial order. This phenomenon can be explained by a combination of the stars' internal structure and the mathematical equations used to model wave propagation. A specific class of modes, defined by their geometric properties rather than their oscillation patterns, has been previously identified but not thoroughly analyzed. However, recent improvements in the treatment of hydrodynamics in astroseismology now allow for a more in-depth examination of these modes using the Euler equation. This approach results in a broader applicability to stars experiencing mass loss or having uneven surface mass distributions. By applying this new framework to solar-like oscillations, a more detailed understanding of the frequency spectrum has been gained, allowing for the interpretation of seismological data in a broader context of stellar physics. This includes the observation that low frequencies may correspond to modes involving circumferential oscillations in the stars' outer layers. This concept has been validated through the analysis of data from the Kepler space telescope, particularly in the case of the star KIC 103111983, which exhibits solar-like oscillations and a significant surface mass dipole structure. This connection holds significant potential for the field of stellar astrophysics, providing a new avenue for the hydrodynamic analysis of static stellar configurations and potentially opening up new areas of research in the field of stellar evolution. We present a novel method that enables the detection of traveling chimera states and synchronized groups within the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of pulse-coupled neural networks. Our approach is systematically robust, as demonstrated across multiple specific network configurations commonly studied in neuroscience, including regular and random wire brain networks, as well as the robust detection of a general synchronized phenomenon in pulse-coupled maps. Furthermore, we find that our method is resistant to imperfect data, offering a valuable tool for the broader scientific community in uncovering important phenomena in complex dynamical systems. Our findings are reported in the accompanying article. We preface that a previous related study existed, but ours surpasses that method in multiple aspects, including the detection of the directed type of synchronization and the requirement for no scaling of variables. We introduce the "standard deviation ratio" technique for our detection method, describing in detail how it yields consistent results across various network configurations and the metrics employed in our analysis. We also explore the relationship between our detection method and the specific time scales used in the evaluation of our results. Additionally, we examine the degree of coexistence and the distinctness of islands in traveling chimera states. We conclude by considering the potential for our method to be applied to the broader field of coupled oscillator networks. We include an open-source implementation of our method in Python, accessible on the GitHub platform. We used this implementation to generate the results presented in the accompanying article. We used the following parameters in our simulations: a = 0.01, b = 0.03, C = 1, D = 1, G = 2, I = 3, N = 100, P = 0.3, R = 20, S = 50, T = 200, V = 10, W = 5, X = 8, Y = 3, Z = 2 for all network configurations except in Figure 4 wherein we set V = 15 and W = 10. We utilized the CSDP library for our least-squares calculations and the NumPy library for all other numerical computations. We successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in the examination of traveling chimera states and synchronized groups within pulse-coupled neural networks and pulse-coupled maps. We made our code publicly available by uploading it to the GitHub repository located at https://github.com/alexsandrosantos/robust-identification-of-synchronized-groups. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous refreshes and conflict-free replication are key techniques for achieving this, but detecting conflicts poses a significant challenge. Our Eliminate-Win design framework streamlines the development of conflict-free replicated data structures by dividing the storage space into segments and assigning each to a single replicator. This approach enables a degree of parallelism that improves performance, and the framework further optimizes conflict detection by implementing a rolling conflict checker. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Eliminate-Win by applying its design principles to build two real-world applications: a memory storage system and a database index. Our evaluation shows that the memory storage system achieves high throughput and low latency, while the database index reduces scan latency by at least 30% and eliminates full-scan operations in three real-world workloads. Additionally, we contribute a formal proof of correctness for the memory storage system and provide practical guidelines for applying the Eliminate-Win framework. As the ATLAS experiment's primary goal is to characterize the Higgs boson's fundamental properties, the Minor Higgs System is essential for achieving this objective. Furthermore, this paper will cover outstanding theoretical predictions related to top-quark pair production and the search for the Standard Model's top-flavor equivalent of the Majoron, a dimensionless scalar that could address electroweak symmetry-breaking problems. In addition to these topics, this paper will also explore prospects for future research at the Large Hadron Collider. This paper focuses on addressing the challenge of unbalanced data in incremental learning, where the aim is to train a neural network on a constantly updating dataset with uneven category distributions. These techniques involve supplementing the predicted instances with additional data by repeating the instances or the missing instances. In order to manufacture reliable and efficient semiconductors, the electronics industry employs a variety of degradations, including random voltage dumping, where manufacturers intentionally reduce the voltage used by a microchip by a certain amount. This technique, known as voltage scaling, enables the production of more effective and energy-efficient processing units. However, it also generates random voltage drops that can lead to random drops in voltage used by the microchip, affecting its performance and efficiency. This research proposes a new method, called Random Voltage Damping Aware Scheduling, which utilizes machine learning algorithms to create efficient timelines for scheduling tasks on processing units affected by random voltage drops. This approach is capable of optimizing performance and energy efficiency on a range of processing units, including CPUs and GPUs, and has been demonstrated on a range of applications, including scientific simulations, machine learning, and multimedia processing. This research also introduces a new metric, called performance isolation factor, which measures the performance impact of random voltage drops on processing units. This study is carried out on a range of processing units and applications obtained from the Stockham dataset and a part of the research has been published in the 2021 ACM Conference on Design, Architecture, and Chips. The proposed method is capable of increasing performance isolation factor by up to 5 times and reducing the performance loss due to random voltage drops by up to 5 times. accurate, yet their performance deteriorates when predicting extreme values. For

less than 1% of images that show violence. This study examines the unusual

insights on their limitations. We observe that models excel at identifying
Intermediate_+ and Intermediate_- categories, but significantly worsen for
Extreme_+ and Extreme_- ones. To account for these variations, we introduce a
new framework that measures the difficulty of predicting certain outcomes based
on the ease of mistaking an extreme class for a default one. This
framework helps identify key factors that affect prediction hardiness, such as
the relationship between attributes and the quality of training data. We also
develop a practical approach to pinpoint rare images that can improve the
robustness of models to out-of-domain data. Our findings are relevant to any
multi-condition classification task, like detecting multiple diseases from
images or text. We hope our research encourages others to explore the
limits of modern machine learning models when dealing with rare outcomes. The

Nonlinear systems like liquid sloshing within a rotating container hold significant practical value in monitoring seismic activity, volatile material storage, and aircraft stability. We introduce the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, a novel sensor design that employs multiple antennas and advanced signal processing techniques to significantly enhance the sensitivity of conventional sensors at high frequencies. We demonstrate the theoretical improvement in sensor response time and showcase the feasibility of the sloshing-Sagnac design using numerical simulations and a prototype of the sensor built from a 1-meter diameter container filled with water. Our results indicate that the sloshing-Sagnac sensor offers a 500 times greater bandwidth than the conventional sensor and a response time that is a hundred times faster in the high frequency range. The paper also explores the effects of various parameters on the sensor's performance and presents a novel algorithm for automating the tuning of the sensor. The paper also provides evidence for the existence of a new phenomenon called resonant wave and proposes the name resonawave for it and, finally, showcases the capability of the sloshing-Sagnac sensor to monitor resonant wave and offers it as a new technology for the detection of gravitational wave. The paper concludes by highlighting the advancements it has brought to gravitational wave technology and the many applications it makes possible, along with a few promising pathways for its further development. The concept of "Big Apple" strength, which represents a critical point in the distribution of matrix elements of one-body and two-body operators in infinite systems, is not widely understood. This article delves into the specifics of this phenomenon and explores its connection to other critical phenomena found in finite systems and cosmic objects. We discuss the distinctive characteristics of wave functions near the Big Apple point and explain why this feature makes the model an effective tool for predicting compact and tightly bound systems, such as finite nuclei and the density distribution in the center of cosmic objects like galaxies. We also examine the relationship between the Big Apple point and other critical phenomena associated with finite systems and cosmic objects that exhibit high degree of stability and that have a small, stable core surrounded by a large, expanding halo. We discuss possible methods for identifying the Big Apple point in systems where the density distribution cannot be directly measured, by looking for the unique patterns of spectroscopic strengths that arise near the Big Apple point. We also discuss the utility of the "strength distribution vs. density" plot as a visual means of recognizing the features of spectroscopic strengths that are indicative of the Big Apple point. We examine potential research opportunities that arise from considering the implications of the Big Apple point, including the possibility that this feature might provide a means of understanding how cosmic objects maintain their stability through nuclear forces. Fujita that presents an alternative mathematical derivation of the critical point, as well as a new figure presented by K. Fujita that illustrates the features of wave functions near the Big Apple point through visual means. This research focuses on creating robust, frequency-stable operations in trapped ion quantum computing by implementing the Molmer-Sorensen gate. To achieve this goal, our method combines multiple low-latitude Gaussian pulses trained on distinct motional modes of the trapped ion. We've developed a fundamental model that explains the molecular behavior and suggested a practical, multi-pulse gate construction based on our findings. By modeling NA62's data collection process and limiting detection errors, we established minimum threshold values for the branching ratio of the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay for three neutral lepton mass categories. Specifically, we found that for a neutral lepton mass between 10 and 500 MeV, the NA62 experiment has the sensitivity to detect a branching ratio as low as $4.5 \times 10^{-10}$. For a neutral lepton mass between 500 and 700 MeV, this sensitivity is achieved at a branching ratio of $2.4 \times 10^{-8}$. Naively extrapolating these findings to the full data collection period, we expect NA62 to achieve these sensitivity thresholds by around 2020. It should be noted that the most stringent limits on the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay set a lower boundary on a neutral lepton mass of approximately 215 MeV. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces two face predictions: one representing the visible facial area and another capturing the hidden aspects. These dual predictions facilitate seamless alignment, even in cases with significantly occluded facial regions. Through extensive testing on the widely used AFLW2000-3D dataset, our method demonstrates enhanced performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, our results show that our proposed framework robustly handles a wide range of head orientations with ease. To further validate the efficacy of our approach, we conduct a systematic analysis of evaluation protocols and find that certain existing methods achieve exceptional performance by exploiting existing mesh templates, often resulting in inaccurate superimposition of reconstructed faces. To address this limitation, we develop an objective evaluation protocol that excludes mesh-based methods, resulting in uniformly improved performance of all evaluated techniques. Our results also indicate a positive correlation between the accuracy of two-dimensional alignment and three-dimensional reconstruction quality. Notably, our method excels in both dimensions. To facilitate thorough investigation, we openly provide all experimental code and configurations. Remarkably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both evaluation protocols, solidifying its position as the top-performing method according to our rigorous evaluation standards. By incorporating a novel bidirectional attention model, previously unassociated speech features can be effectively extracted and the influence of noisy background suppressed. This phenomenon occurs in nickel when an x-ray photon is absorbed, causing a pivotal state to interact with a competing state and, within a femtosecond timescale, return to its ground state. A simplified global circulation model is examined to understand why it exhibits varying rotation speeds, regardless of the imposed rotation rate in the outer atmosphere. This phenomenon is common in models of planets with weak rotation and low gravity, yet it's unlike the circulation patterns observed on Earth and other rapidly rotating terrestrial planets. In search of answers, researchers studied a model that includes a narrow, fast-moving jet stream and a wide, slow-moving atmosphere, and found that this two-speed circulation pattern emerges when the model's horizontal and vertical scales are significantly unequal. This outcome is linked to the presence of scale-dependent instability and transition to turbulence at a specific horizontal scale, which is determined by the planet's rotation rate and influences the scale at which energy is transferred across the atmosphere. This result implies that fast-moving jet streams are an intrinsic feature of the circulation systems found on planets with weak rotation and low gravity, and suggests that these jet streams should be stable features, without the need for additional factors such as excessive entropy or interior heat sources. Furthermore, this research may provide insights useful for studying Earth's atmospheric circulation, particularly during its early formation when the Sun's energy and the interior of the Earth were less mature. In follow-up studies, the effects of increasing the complexity of the model's physics and the introduction of baroclinic instability are explored in further detail. This includes an analysis of the parameters influencing the scale of turbulence in the model, as well as a comparison of the results to observations on Mars and the gas giants. Additionally, a numerical model is developed to mimic the behavior of the simple model, and a new framework for classifying planetary circulation systems is proposed, positioning Earth's as intermediate, geostrophic turbulence. This classification is based on the rotation rate, gravity, and atmospheric scale length parameters, and is shown to link the behavior of the simple model to that of more complex numerical models and observations on various planets. This includes fast cyclostrophic super-rotation on small, rapidly rotating terrestrial planets, geostrophic turbulence on intermediate-sized planets like Mars, and stable jet streams on large gas giants. This research may have implications for the study of planetary evolution, as the formation of atmospheric circulation systems and planetary temperatures may be closely linked to rotation rate and gravity through their effects on turbulence and energy transfer across the atmosphere. This, in turn, could influence the habitability of a planet, making it an important area for further investigation. This study discloses novel analytical and geometrical aspects of the generalized algebraic multiplicity of a polynomial, initially introduced in \cite{GHOSAL202 Foster}. We initially unveil a groundbreaking formula that calculates this expanded multiplicity for polynomials of any degree, thereby surpassing the limitation to binomial coefficients inherent in the conventional approach. Furthermore, we establish a significant connection between the generalized multiplicity and the geometric distribution of roots on a complex plane, ultimately leveraging this relationship to derive our analytical formula. Specifically, we show that the generalized multiplicity is directly proportional to the total angular measure of sectors of the complex plane excluded from root locations, effectively utilizing this exclusion to formulate the polynomial's reciprocal polynomial in terms of its original roots. We explore various scenarios of root distribution to illustrate the practical applications of our analytical formula, and we introduce an innovative reciprocal polynomial recurrence framework that is both efficient and versatile. Lastly, we investigate an intriguing link between the generalized multiplicity and the geometric arrangement of roots in the complex plane for polynomials of degree three. Additionally, we introduce an innovative indexing system for roots that is both intuitive and harmoniously aligned with the algebraic structure of polynomials. Ultimately, we establish that this expanded multiplicity captures the intrinsic properties of polynomials comprehensively, providing a universal framework that encompasses various specialized multiplicity measures commonly employed in distinct mathematical contexts. This study's findings are particularly significant in the context of random polynomial analysis, particularly when employing the Lyubarskii distribution, as they offer an advanced multiplicity measure that is both a natural extension and a critical differentiation from existing theories. Conversely, we also identify key limitations in our understanding that these advanced multiplicity measures face challenges in being directly quantified in geometric terms. Nonetheless, our study's contributions provide substantial insights that can be applied across a broader range of problems involving polynomial roots. On a broader theoretical level, our study's results are shown to be a natural fit for the more universal concepts introduced in the recent paper by the same authors presented at the 2023 ICML conference. Ultimately, our study's findings are expected to have a positive impact on the broader community working on problems related to polynomial roots. Notably, the Hall anomaly's rise is more pronounced in higher-quality crystals with lower residual resistivity, indicating that the vacancy distribution within the vortex state is sensitive to the underlying material's properties. The model demonstrates accuracy in predicting the Hall anomaly's magnitude based on the normal state's transport properties. We also examine the influence of applied magnetic field on the Hall anomaly, observing a decrease in its magnitude below a critical field strength, which we attribute to a normalization effect influenced by high-field resistivity and the resulting increase in normalized Hall resistance. The interplay between these factors is shown to result in a minimum in the Hall anomaly's magnitude. We propose a novel, human-in-the-loop multi-agent approach that incorporates a rating system, where users evaluate the model's performance and provide confidence levels for their predictions. A separate agent identifies and amplifies high-confidence, accurate predictions to refine the model using optimized data, resulting in enhanced performance and reduced instability. We showcase this method's effectiveness through a simulation experiment and an empirical study on a real-world dataset. Our results demonstrate that our proposed system outperforms traditional data augmentation methods and matches the model's original performance, even when only a small percentage of users engage with the rating system. Furthermore, we find that incorporating user feedback leads to improved model robustness in both simulated and real-world scenarios. We make available our code and the tested dataset on GitHub. Overall, our proposed human-in-the-loop approach provides an innovative solution to the challenge of ensuring artificial intelligence reliability. Additionally, we believe this method to be a pioneering example of collaborative work between machine learning and multi-agent research. As a result, we hope this approach will be considered a reference point for other researchers exploring ways to enhance the reliability of machine learning models.

In recent years, various organizations have experienced security threats due to the illegal transportation of prohibited items, leading them to rely heavily on X-ray security scanning. Although advances in computer vision have improved prohibited item detection, there is a significant gap between in-lab and real-world scanning accuracy. Factors contributing to this disparity include inadequate training datasets, insufficient data normalization, and the inability of current models to mitigate artificial enhancements to the image. As a result, security teams are increasingly relying on human validation of scanned images, a time-consuming and inefficient process. To address these challenges, we introduce a high-standard benchmark consisting of 5,000 meticulously annotated images, along with a novel lateral inhibition module that effectively mitigates image enhancement artifacts. This module employs a combination of spatial and channel-wise normalization techniques to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and achieves notable improvements in model robustness and real-world evaluation accuracy. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of our lateral inhibition module in augmenting model diversity and adapting to other computer vision tasks. Our benchmark and module offer valuable contributions to the field of prohibited item detection, while also highlighting potential applications and research directions for future work. As security scanning is a critically important topic, we encourage the community to build upon our findings and advancements. Additionally, we provide comprehensive guidelines for maintaining and expanding the benchmark, alongside a benchmark-specific evaluation metric that prioritizes high-standard data quality. This initiative aims to accelerate progress in prohibited item detection and secure scanning beyond just digital platform data. As such, we believe it will also benefit other high-challenge computer vision tasks characterized by limited data, real-world diversification, and the presence of artificial manipulations. Achieving comprehensive security coverage with traditional testing methods is increasingly difficult due to the sophistication of modern vulnerabilities. This problem is exacerbated by the limited number of publicly available vulnerabilities. To address this challenge, this paper suggests utilizing previously discovered vulnerabilities as a diverse test suite for a given target, such as an application or protocol. This approach is referred to as the "Diverse Test Suite" method. Our evaluation of this approach includes a diverse test suite made up of 1,549 previously discovered vulnerabilities across 10 targets, which was used to train and evaluate the effectiveness of various fuzzing and testing techniques. Our results indicate that the diverse test suite yields a significantly higher detection rate compared to other test suites. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the diversity of the test suite has a direct impact on the effectiveness of these techniques. To facilitate future research, we have openly disseminated the diverse test suites and our methodology for creating them. Furthermore, our work offers a framework for assessing and comparing the coverage and efficacy of different testing and fuzzing methods. This assessment is performed through a variety of metrics, including diversity, reachability, uniqueness, and binary coverage. Our data highlights the importance of diversity in test cases and indicates that other metrics may not always correlate with practical success in activating and exploiting vulnerabilities. Our research demonstrates the value of diverse test cases in evaluating the robustness of security in applications and protocols. This benefit extends beyond vulnerability activation, as diverse test cases can facilitate detection of security-related issues by static analysis, improve the effectiveness of compression-based obfuscation detection, and enhance the efficiency of protocol performance evaluation. Our work has significant implications for the field of security testing, suggesting that diversity is a crucial factor to achieve comprehensive security coverage. This insight is relevant not only to the evaluation of fuzzers but also to the development of effective testing and testing-related technologies, as diversity is a crucial property to attain in this domain. Our research has been theoretically supported and empirically validated, which provides a clear roadmap for future research in this area. Machine learning models are frequently tested with cross-validation to ensure their performance is reliable, however, a common issue arises when evaluating models for natural language processing tasks. The technique we propose, K-fold jackknife cross-validation, aims to address this problem by combining results from conventional K-fold and jackknife methods. This approach filters out variance by prioritizing the simplest method (jackknife) while maintaining the ability to estimate model performance variability (K-fold). We demonstrate the efficacy of this technique by applying it to three NLP datasets and show that it yields more stable evaluations than conventional K-fold cross-validation. The code and further details are available at https://github.com/linuslau/jk-fold-xval. Furthermore, we explore the potential of modifying this approach to accommodate diverse evaluation needs and suggest future research directions for NLP model evaluation. The traditional cross-validation methods have limitations when evaluating sequential machine learning models, including natural language processing tasks that often involve systematic changes from one instance to the next. This issue arises because each prediction significantly influences the input for the next iteration, either in a document or a conversation. As a result, models performing well on individual instances may not guarantee them to perform equally well across the entire sequence. The conventional cross-validation techniques fall into this pitfall, leading to an overestimation of the model's performance. This note explores an alternative approach called the K-jackknife cross-validation method, which combines the advantages of both techniques to provide a more precise estimate of model performance. This method prioritizes the simpler jackknife method for estimating the expected performance and utilizes conventional K-fold cross-validation to gauge the variation in this estimate. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to three NLP datasets and show that it yields more stable evaluations than conventional K-fold cross-validation. The code and further details are available at https://github.com/linuslau/jk-fold-xval. As models continue to evolve with increasing complexity, it is essential to reevaluate the conventional cross-validation methods used for model evaluation. Our results suggest that the proposed K-jackknife cross-validation method is a more reliable alternative, and we believe it is worthy of further investigation. This relationship holds universal value, applicable to all WIMP targets. Additionally, we have established that the scattering angle is directly proportional to the recoil energy and incident speed. We have created practical tables and graphs to guide researchers in interpreting WIMP data, including those involved in the LUXe experiment. Our analysis demonstrates that measuring the scattering angle's distribution at high recoil energies can significantly improve the effectiveness of WIMP detection. We have also introduced a new statistical method for evaluating WIMP evidence based on the scattering angle's distribution. This approach surpasses conventional methods by providing a more comprehensive assessment of data and identifying potential biases. It ends with considerations for the next-generation WIMP experiments, emphasizing the importance of accurately measuring the scattering angle's distribution. This study aims to investigate this effect and gauge the likelihood of users missing pertinent information due to personalization. To achieve this, the research introduces a new metric called "perceptual precision," which indicates the proportion of conspicuous relevant information users are aware of. To assess this metric, the study designs two key experiments to determine its components and factors influencing it. The results show that users are likely to overlook pertinent information due to personalization and that certain user characteristics, such as search expertise and confidence in ratings, influence their perception of relevance. Furthermore, the study finds that the overall precision of users' searches is a key factor in their perceptual precision. To address the limitation of previous studies on this topic, the research also examines the relationship between users' actual and perceived accuracy, as well as the impact of search expertise on this relationship. The fundamental limitations of present particle accelerators can be understood by looking at the achievements of the LHC. Due to the necessity for higher energies to recognize or deny new physics, future colliders will need to surpass the performance of their predecessors. The proposed μIoC (Muon-Ion Collider) is one such future collider that has the unique ability to provide both extremely high energy muon collisions and a powerful proton-proton colliding beam capability at a relatively low cost. This paper will delve into the scientific justification behind choosing a Muon-Ion Collider and present an initial design for this accelerator, with a focus on the proton-proton section. Ultimately, we demonstrate that this design can achieve a significant fraction of the LHC's peak performance in both proton-proton and heavy ion collisions. As a result, μIoC has the potential to become an influential particle accelerator in the future. The proposed design, however, is not optimized for proton-proton collisions and there are several areas where enhancements can be made through various beam focus improvement methods. We also provide an indication of the potential for heavy ion collisions at increased beam intensities, beyond what is achievable with today's technology. Furthermore, we explore the possibilities of incorporating a $50\,\text{GeV}$ electron storage ring into the Muon-IoC design, which could lead to the discovery of a long-sought phenomenon or provide a significant improvement in the sensitivity of a planned electron ionizer. This paper is an invitation for the broader particle physics community to engage with the Muon-IoC concept and contribute to the discussion on the future direction of hadron colliders. We look forward to receiving feedback on our proposal and encourage everyone to join the conversation. This investigation examines the paired permutation tests employed in modern statistical analysis, particularly in relation to randomised sampling methods. Our key finding indicates that the accuracy of confidence intervals and hypothesis test performance suffers significantly when using paired permutations in cases where the data exhibits an underlying structure. Our results demonstrate a clear advantage of alternative testing methods, such as the exact distribution approach or bootstrap methods, over paired permutations. Furthermore, we establish that the risk of inaccurate results increases in proportion to the square of the size of the data structure. Our research also provides guidelines for data analysts on when to expect a data structure to impact test performance and suggests a simple algorithm for identifying such structures. Our findings are illustrated through a series of simulations as well as a real-world application to a genetic study. Our study has important implications for the statistical analysis of data in various fields, including medicine, psychology, biology, and finance. We propose an alternative approach, based on the idea of shellable posets, to examine the faces of a certain geometric structure known as a polytopical scheme. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging node and edge features to outcomes. Yet, their versatility can be limited by their reliance on extensive training data and detailed feature configurations. To break through this constraint, we develop a novel approach called ASNet, which combines sparse graph pruning with neural network training. By achieving a balance between efficient computation and accurate performance, ASNet outperforms existing methods while requiring a mere 1/5 of previous approaches for neural network parameters. On the Mayo Clinic Corpus dataset, ASNet achieves a remarkable 5.3% improvement in micro-precision and 8.3% increase in micro-recall over baseline models, ultimately resulting in a 12% improvement in F1-score. Moreover, ASNet enables easier analysis of GNN outcomes by condensing critical information onto edges within a sparse subgraph. ASNet's effectiveness is further validated across multiple open-source code frameworks and our source code is available for public access. ASNet demonstrates a pioneering strategy for training interpretable and efficient GNN models. Additionally, ASNet's code is now available online at https://github.com/jayantndotme/ASNet. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at capturing dot product information and identifying the largest vector. Its key benefit lies in its efficiency, as it only requires a single pass over the data and minimal storage, making it suitable for large-scale applications. However, the count sketch method falls short in situations where the query depends on previous data, as documented in previous research. In this paper, we investigate a more general setting where the query adapts to the given sketch and provide a lower bound for $\phi$, the failure probability of CountSketch, showing it to be at least on the order of $R^2 \div (\beta^2 \cdot k)$ for specific values of $k$, $R$, and $\beta$. Notably, this lower bound aligns with the known upper bounds for specific cases, such as $k=1$ and $R=\Omega(\sqrt{\beta^2 \cdot k})$. To establish this lower bound, we introduced a new family of hash functions and proved their performance relative to $k$, $R$, and $\beta$. Moreover, we propose an enhanced version of CountSketch called CountSketch-Skew, tailored to handle imbalanced frequencies. CountSketch-Skew exhibits an improved failure probability of $R^2 \div (\beta^2 \cdot k^2)$, outperforming previous remedies. Notably, its performance gains over the basic CountSketch surpass those of prior methods. We have formally analyzed the theoretical performance of CountSketch under various scenarios, including both adaptive and non-adaptive settings. Furthermore, we provide concrete implementations of CountSketch Sketch, including a basic count sketch and count sketch variants, making them publicly available for reference. Finally, we verify the effectiveness of CountSketch Sketch through comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets in both low-frequency and high-frequency contexts. The results show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in all tested scenarios. The enhanced performer, CountSketch-Skew, delivers superior performance in every experiment. We have explored a significant extension of CountSketch called MultiSketch, involving a collection of independent count sketch modules. We establish a lower bound for the failure probability of $k$ independent sketches as $R^2 \div (\beta^2)$$, indicating a linear decrease in the required number of sketches. We have experimentally validated the performance of MultiSketch across various datasets and scenarios. Building on previous work, we developed a strategy to break down a manifold's total scalar curvature into non-negative components in the presence of certain minimal topological features. However, this approach was hindered by the possibility of singular points arising from the removal of certain manifolds. In the current study, we establish methods for locally removing such singularities resulting from the set $\mathcal{W}$ and similarly those from $\mathcal{S}$, enabling us to decompose the total scalar curvature across the remaining smooth components of our original manifold. Furthermore, we explore specific situations where these techniques allow us to separate the manifold's volume into distinct parts regulated by set $\mathcal{S}$, and in set $\mathcal{W}$ we find ways to achieve the optimal configuration where one component dominates the remaining parts. Lastly, we discuss an alternative approach for merging components of our manifolds while closely examining the effects on scalar curvature and related geometric features. This includes establishing conditions under which a linear combination of a pair of spheres will result in a manifold with non-negative scalar curvature. In addition, we identify certain instances in which our methods for analyzing set $\mathcal{S}$ and set $\mathcal{W}$ apply, thereby further generalizing our initial decomposition strategy. 
  To generalize further, we need to consider other geometric conditions defined by closed sets and examine how these impact the curvature of associated manifolds. This leads us to introduce a new condition based on geodesic paths, which enables us to break down the total scalar curvature of a manifold into non-negative components, extending our initial decomposition strategy to a broader range of manifolds. 
  However, this new condition may introduce singularities in a manner more complex than their analogues in sets $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{W}$. Yet, we are able to eliminate these singularities locally, thereby successfully applying our strategy to a broader range of manifolds. This has significant implications, as for instance it enables us to separate the volume of a manifold into components controlled by sets defined by geodesic paths and controls the growth of the curvature of certain manifolds near their conical points. Moreover, we are able to demonstrate the existence of minimal surfaces with specific geometric features and we can merge components of a manifold in a way that affects its scalar curvature and related geometric features. This holds a significant generalization over our previous work and greatly expands our understanding of the relationships between geometry, topology and analysis in a broad range of manifolds.

This implication leads to a complex relationship between vortex dynamics, characterized by chiral gauge fields, and the inherent entropy of the superfluid. As a result, the entropy of the superfluid is directly linked to its ability to resist the beamed vortex impulse, which is a self-interacting impulse due to the superfluid's unique properties. Consequently, the beamed vortex impulse can only effectively induce a response in the superfluid if its self-interaction is overcome, resulting in a response that is a response time that is a fraction of a millisecond. Notably, this response time varies based on the carrier density of the superconducting material, which dictates the mean free path of the superfluid's constituent quasiparticles. We introduce a novel learning-driven predictive control method called
Aggregate Adaptability (AA), an innovative approach that leverages
machine learning to efficiently manage large-scale complex systems involving
multiple interconnected agents. Our key contribution is in developing a
general framework for optimizing the performance of systems characterized by
adaptive random networks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach
by applying it to the control of a multi-agent system featuring adaptive
random graphs. Our key finding is that our approach achieves a comparable
degree of performance to more sophisticated methods requiring extensive
system information, while doing so at a significantly lower computational
cost. Furthermore, we show that our approach is particularly well-suited
for systems with limited communication between agents. We also explore the
application of our approach to the control of systems involving random
changes, describing an effective method for updating the learned model.
Our results and methodology are particularly relevant to the control of
power grids managed by energy management systems (EMS). We demonstrate
the efficacy of our approach on a simulated test case based on the IEEE
30-node grid system. All of our code is openly accessible on the Gym website

In this paper, we present SCATTER, a novel computational framework that leverages machine learning for simulating the interaction of compact accretors with intact envelopes in post-mass-accretion phases, including main-sequence binaries and compact binaries with neutron star or black hole companions. By generating a large set of model spectra drawn from critical parameters, SCATTER delivers a user-friendly interface for analyzing observational data and extracting physical characteristics of these systems. The framework excels in handling a large number of parameters influencing the spectrum, such as mass, spin, accretion rate, and temperature. SCATTER accurately models the spectrum in a data-driven manner, bypassing the necessity for solving complex radiative transfer equations. The inferred parameters are comparable to those obtained from other methods, yet SCATTER yields results in a significantly shorter computation time. Furthermore, SCATTER identifies minimal parameter sets that control the spectral output, eliminating unnecessary variables and speeding up the optimization process. This study evaluates the effectiveness of next-generation electron-positron colliders at detecting double Higgs production, considering a wide range of scenarios involving Effective Field Theories and Higgs boson interactions beyond the Standard Model. Calculations account for several EFT configurations, including Higgs contact terms, a Higgs mass matrix, and a Higgs effective field for itself. Edge computing enables fast, user-friendly interactions between individuals and technology by reducing latency from central servers. However, the reliability of these systems is compromised due to the difficulty of conducting comprehensive testing in real-world environments. Our approach addresses this challenge by focusing on the specific events that users experience, such as scanning a QR code or receiving in-app notifications. We develop an event-focused testing framework to identify and model these events, including the underlying conditions and potential exceptions that can occur. By pinpointing critical points in the application development life cycle, we can integrate testing into our process through techniques like differential testing and fault injection. Our approach is exemplified through the enhancement of a popular file-sharing application, showcasing how event-focused testing can be applied in practice. Our findings highlight the value of our approach and the common issues that developers face when implementing it in their daily work. Finally, we provide directions for further research in this area, including the integration of machine learning and natural language processing to enhance our event-focused testing framework. Our work is relevant to the broader field of reliable software development, as well as the specific challenges and opportunities presented by edge computing and Internet of Things applications.

The development of highly advanced and safe self-driving vehicles relies heavily on realistic traffic simulation tools.  Current approaches often focus on incorporating individual components that mimic real-world elements but lack overall coherence and accuracy.  To address this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a novel system that utilizes a comprehensive scene representation and employs a method called sorted neighbor selection to choose high-quality features for modeling traffic scenes.  SceneGen leverages a vast public database of annotated traffic scenes and utilizes a multi-stage process involving both global and local feature extraction to accurately depict scene elements and their interrelationships.  To further enhance realism, SceneGen uses a semantic coherence metric that assesses and refines the model's understanding of scene context, ensuring a more realistic representation of traffic scenarios.  We demonstrate SceneGen's effectiveness by comparing its simulations to real-world scenes captured through a mounted camera system and show that our method outperforms existing traffic simulation approaches.  We also offer your access to our code and dataset available at https://github.com/oldtownmap/scenegen.  We hope this work contributes meaningfully to the development of more realistic and versatile traffic simulation tools essential for refining and testing autonomous vehicle software.  Additionally, we propose an extended version of the system that utilizes generative neural networks, aptly named SceneGan, tailored to generate unique non-realistic scene configurations suitable for testing and evaluation of self-driving vehicle algorithms.  We believe this variation holds promise and warrants further exploration in the field of computer vision.  We look forward to your feedback on this research and encourage its further development. This prediction complements a previous method for calculating the self-energy in doped graphene and enables us to derive a non-linear response to an applied electric field at finite temperatures. Furthermore, we relate the screening to the thermal capacity of doped graphene and demonstrate that our shielding approach is consistent with this thermal capacity. Additionally, we investigate the impact of temperature on the spectral function and quasi-particle weight. Our model may be applicable to other two-dimensional systems with strong interactions. We also provide a thermal capacitance formula that can be used for general screened interactions. This is particularly relevant for the strong-coupling regime in doped graphene, where a previous method breaks down. Our results suggest that the capacitance in this regime is proportional to the charge carrier density. We have previously demonstrated that strong-coupling effects are common in doped graphene due to the strong electron-electron interactions and low density of states. Consequently, the thermal capacitance of doped graphene is primarily linear, with a small nonlinear component arising from the interaction strength. We have previously shown that the zero-temperature shielding in doped graphene is extensive, meaning it involves the entire system, although the capacity to do so is weakened at finite temperatures. This phenomenon may be related to the recently observed extended Heisenberg spin chains in doped graphene. We propose an experimental verification of our theoretical model by measuring the thermal dependence of the screening and spectral function at the graphene's epitaxial growth interface versus depth. This can be achieved by adjusting the substrate concentration and/or introducing defects that create diverse electron states with varying temperatures, potentially switching between extensive and non-extensive screening. This is because optical conductivity is a surface-layered effect, similar to screening and spectral function. However, the impact of temperature on optical conductivity is less pronounced due to the larger energy gap between optical transitions. Consequently, the screening in doped graphene is primarily driven by the extensive thermal dependence of the capacity rather than optical absorption.
