A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, where the main task is processed through a series of refinement frames, with each frame obtained from an upsampled previous frame. However, this method leads to aliasing and distortion due to the upsampling of motion-blurred images. To address this issue, a non-aliasing technique called sub-pixel interpolation was developed but only considers neighboring frames with similar directions of motion. As a result, this method fails to account for more complex motion patterns, leading to artifacts in the reconstructed frames. To overcome these limitations, a new algorithm called BasicVSR++ is proposed, where the refinement frame is obtained from an accurate estimation of the blurred frame rather than the upsampled previous frame. This estimation is achieved through motion estimation and warp, resulting in a more precise reconstruction of the frame. To increase efficiency, a novel single-frame estimator was developed, which provides a direct solution to the non-aliasing reconstruction of the frame. This estimator uses a multi-layer feature of the upsampled previous frame to estimate the super-resolved frame, followed by a reverse warp to obtain the estimated blurred frame. BasicVSR++ was evaluated against state-of-the-art methods on commonly used datasets, demonstrating its superiority in video super-resolution tasks. The source code of the proposed algorithm is also made publicly available. As an additional exploration, a set of challenging video super-resolution tasks was constructed to highlight the limitations of existing approaches and the advantages of the novel estimator. These challenges demonstrate the difficulties encountered when processing videos with complex motion patterns, large scale factors, and low-quality frames. To further improve the performance on these challenging tasks, a novel loss function called structural progressive loss was introduced, aiming to preserve the structural information at each upsampled layer. However, the evaluation shows that even with this optimized loss function, the existing state-of-the-art methods continue to struggle with these challenging videos. Therefore, further research is needed to fully address these complex video super-resolution tasks. The code of the proposed algorithm BasicVSR++ is made available at https://github.com/lingcacala/BasicVSRpp. Additionally, the challenge datasets are available at https://github.com/lingcacala/VideoSuperResolutionChallenges.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, highly related skills are learned from rewards generated by multiple shared environments. We analyze how the interaction between tasks affects learning and observe that in certain situations, the similarity in reward signals can cause one skill to hinder the learning of another. To address this, we present a modular multi-task reinforcement learning approach that minimizes the negative impact of destructive interference. This method leverages separate world models for each task, allowing the policy networks to focus on combining the information from different environments. When the world models are shared, a novel modular multi-task reinforcement learning framework learns multiple policy networks and a single world model for each environment, while preventing the interference between policy networks. When the world models are distinct, the framework uses a shared value function to guide the learning of multiple policy networks, and a module-specific target policy technique reduces destructive interference. Our results show that the proposed method outperforms existing multi-task reinforcement learning methods in complex problems. The code is available at https://github.com/ghm-ai/mtmrl. The theoretical analysis of the approach is outlined in the appendix. The paper is currently under review for publication at the 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021). It has also been presented at the 34th Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AI21) and the 2nd Workshop on Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MultiAgent21). This study utilizes scintillation observations of the bright pulsar B1133+16 to gather spatial and spectral information about the intervening plasma. Unlike most pulsars, B1133+16's scintillation pattern shows a distinct, narrow "bridge" of increased interference, which scientists attribute to a dense plasma structure bridging two separate ionization bubbles around neutron stars. This phenomenon is unusual because it forms over a significant frequency range, approximately 1 GHz to 1.5 GHz, unlike the typical narrow frequency bands associated with geometric scintillation. Based on very large array observations, a detailed model of this plasma structure has been developed, revealing a bridge composed of narrowband geometric scintillation and a surrounding area with wideband diffraction scintillation, both connected at a critical density threshold. This model predicts a minimal width of approximately 0.14 parsecs (or 130 astronomical units) where scintillation is most active and a curved scintillation pattern caused by a nearby ionized region surrounding the neutron star. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have excelled in various tasks due to their flexibility in handling complex and dynamic graph data. Current GNN models operate within a Euclidean framework but have a significant limitation - they cannot effectively represent time and other directional relationships. Our proposal, Lorentzian GNNs, breaks through this constraint by introducing a new relational modeling framework rooted in differential geometry. Lorentzian GNNs treat graphs as topological structures embedded in a differential manifold and leverage their intrinsic geometric properties to enhance GNN performance. Our approach is highly versatile, making it compatible with existing GNN architectures by simply replacing their convolutional modules with Lorentzian counterparts. A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing undirected graph, effectively creating a variant of the original graph using a binary operation. In this context, we explore the concept of an extended double cover in relation to a graph's signed variant. Essentially, an x-distribution on a graph H refers to a specific mapping that identifies subsets of H's vertices as being part of an "x" group, where this labeling is analogous to the polarity used in signed graphs. We then establish that a graph's x-distribution exists if, and only if, there is a homomorphism available from a specific variant of a target graph to the original graph. Building on this foundation, we identify conditions under which different types of x-distributions are equivalent, and we also introduce a new framework that broadens the scope of homomorphism-related concepts to their relationship with the symmetries present in twisted graphs. This theoretical framework is subsequently applied to several key instances, including its connection to the concept of twin-free graphs and graph minors, and we also establish that a number of variants of certain types of graphs, such as trees and minor-minors, can be represented as a combination of an underlying structure and a specific x-distribution. Furthermore, we introduce an associated order-theoretic limit generalizing the concept of homomorphism-preserving functions to twisted graphs, and we demonstrate that this order-theoretic limit is equivalent to the natural representation of a graph's x-distribution. Additionally, we discuss the applicability of our results to areas such as graph coloring and the stability number of a graph. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting potential research extensions and the underlying connections to other mathematical concepts.
